subject: Reducing ingress surface: VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs Site-to-Site (decision inputs)
messages:
From: Tim Wu <tim.wu@acme-analytics.com>
To: kimberly_park@redwood.com
Cc: claire.johnson@finexa.com
Date: Thu, 9 Jul 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Private deploy connectivity — minimize public surface, low-latency requirement

Kimberly,

Quick background: Acme is evaluating Redwood Private with a short inference tail for fraud models (p99 latency target ~70ms to 150ms depending on request size). Security requires minimizing public IP exposure and providing a narrow ingress surface for our production VPCs. Options on the table from our side: VPC Peering (direct), PrivateLink / interface endpoints, and an IPsec S2S VPN to our onprem edge.

Could you help run a short recommendation: when to prefer peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S (with pros/cons), rough operational complexity, and any constraints that would push us to choose one over another? We're particularly worried about:
- Attack surface (public IPs and routable prefixes)
- Cross-account IAM/service identity implications
- Multi-region failover and latency consistently under 150ms
- Egress/cost implications (data transfer fees)

Happy to share our network team calendar for a quick sync — Claire is on this thread and can add context on routing and firewall posture.

Thanks,

—Tim
Tim Wu
NetOps Lead, Acme Analytics

From: kimberly_park@redwood.com
To: Tim Wu <tim.wu@acme-analytics.com>
Cc: marcus_lin@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com, soojin_lee@redwood.com, claire.johnson@finexa.com

Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity — minimize public surface, low-latency requirement

Tim — thanks for the clear ask. I pulled together a concise decision matrix and a recommended next-step plan (attached). High level summary first, then quick bullets mapping to your constraints.

Quick recommendation (tl;dr):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) as the default for production-grade private deploys when minimizing public routable surface is the primary driver and the application traffic is HTTP(s)-based.
- VPC Peering when absolute lowest hop-count and lowest sustained latency are required and both sides can accept full route propagation / broader CIDR exposure across accounts.
- IPsec S2S VPN as a fallback when the customer cannot use provider-managed interface endpoints or for hybrid on-prem -> cloud sites where BGP and dedicated circuits are not feasible. Use S2S only with strict ACLs and anti-spoofing controls.

How this maps to your constraints:
- Attack surface: PrivateLink avoids advertising customer CIDRs into Redwood's network and prevents us from needing public IPs on our service endpoint. Peering exposes both sides to larger L3 surface via accepted routes. VPN keeps things isolated but relies on the tunnel endpoint being hardened and reachable.
- IAM/service identity: PrivateLink maps naturally to per-account ENIs and security groups; we can restrict endpoint policies by principal and service. Peering relies more on network-based ACLs and is less granular at the service identity layer.
- Multi-region failover: Peering can be stretched with transit or inter-region peering but becomes operationally heavier. PrivateLink can be fronted by a regional failover strategy (regional endpoints + DNS routing) — adds some complexity but keeps surface area small.
- Cost: PrivateLink carries per-ENI/hour and per-GB data processing charges. Peering transfers (intra-cloud) sometimes cheaper for high-volume low-latency flows. VPN has bandwidth limits and potential egress fees; also more ops cost for tunnel maintenance.

Operational complexity and suggested plan:
1) Quick PoC: Create a PrivateLink endpoint in your prod VPC and run a synthetic latency test to our Private deployment in us-west-2. (low effort, preserves security posture)
2) If measured latency is above your requirement, evaluate a peering trial between a dedicated Redwood VPC and your prod VPC in the same AZ/region (we can shadow traffic, limited route exposure)
3) If onprem strictures force it, define a hardened IPsec profile (esp. IKEv2, strong ciphers) and use VPN with precise ACLs and monitoring.

I attached: redwood-conn-matrix-v1.xlsx (matrix w/ tradeoffs), private-deploy-diagram.png (simplified topology).

Next steps: Marcus and Karthik — can you add any low-level kernel/kv-cache/latency implications for each pattern? Soojin — please summarize any AWS/GCP-specific constraints we need to call out. Tim/Claire — if you can share a sample p99 RTT from a known agent to your prod VPC, we can sketch better latency guidance.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Senior Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity — latency & perf notes

Adding technical context from the runtime perspective. Short bullets:

- Latency profile: For small prompt sizes where token generation dominates, network latency becomes a larger fraction of p99. Peering typically gives lowest median and tail (remove NAT/managed hops). PrivateLink adds one extra ENI hop but is still usually within ~5-12ms of peering inside a region depending on AZ placement.
- KV cache and batching: If you plan cross-VPC batching or shared prefix caching, peering makes cache-coherency and cross-VPC bursting simpler. PrivateLink isolates the dataplane per-account which can complicate cache-sharing unless we run a shared service within your account (more ops).
- TLS termination & mutual auth: PrivateLink allows us to terminate within the provider network and map to internal service instances; mutual TLS + endpoint policies are recommended. Peering requires stricter mutual authentication at the application layer since it relies on L3 connectivity.
- Observability: VPN tunnels add extra path opacity; debugging tail latencies across IPsec can be painful (MTU, rekeying events).

My operational suggestion: Start with PrivateLink PoC. If your synthetic numbers show >20ms additional tail vs peering, run a constrained peering test for a slice of traffic and measure real tail behavior with a production-like load. If you need cache-coherent shared state at low latency, peering will likely win.

—Marcus
Marcus Lin
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity — cost & governance notes

A few operational and governance notes to surface:

- Route leakage risk (peering): With peering you need strict route filters and tagging to avoid accidental CIDR advertisement between non-target accounts. For customers that must guarantee strict tenancy separation (audit/compliance), peering can be problematic unless you build transit VPC boundaries.
- Endpoint lifecycle (PrivateLink): ENIs are governed by the customer account; we recommend a small runbook for endpoint rotation and security group review. Endpoint policy enforcement is the recommended control for least privilege.
- VPN lifecycle: Plan for rekey windows, monitoring for packet drops, and escalation playbooks. If customer wants an air-gapped-ish posture, IPsec + strict ACLs is the only path without provider-managed endpoints but it increases mean-time-to-repair for incidents.
- Cost predictability: PrivateLink costs are easier to forecast per-endpoint; peering data transfer costs can spike with cross-AZ/cloud egress. VPN bandwidth costs may be lower for small volumes but operational time is higher.

If Acme's security/compliance team wants to disallow any route exchange into their routing tables, PrivateLink is the safe default. If they explicitly allow managed peering and need the lowest tail latency, we can accommodate but will request a scoped peering with ACLs and a limited CIDR set.

—Karthik

Appreciate the clear framework — that helps. Two quick clarifications and a path-forward:

1) Surface requirements: Acme security has confirmed they will not accept route imports into their VPC routing tables that contain third-party prefixes. That effectively rules out broad peering unless we can guarantee no route leakage.
2) Latency: We'll run the PrivateLink PoC you suggested and collect p95/p99 numbers under a synthetic load. If PoC shows >25ms tail overhead compared to our internal baseline, we'll revisit scoped peering but only for a narrow AZ pair and with explicit route-filtering and monitoring.

Please schedule a 30-min call next week to kick off the PrivateLink PoC and the required IAM/endpoint-policy templates. Claire will push a calendar invite. Also — please attach the sample endpoint policy and minimal SG examples to the shared drive link you posted.

Thanks everyone — looking forward to the PoC.
